turns.prompt_text: I'd like to now install ollama on my mac mini
turns.response_html:
Setting up Ollama on an Apple Silicon Mac Mini is a fantastic choice—the unified memory handles local LLMs beautifully.

Here is the straightforward guide to getting it up and running, along with a few terminal-centric tips for your workflow.

Installation Methods

Method 1: The Quick Terminal Installer (Recommended)

You can pipe the official install script directly into your shell. Open your terminal and run:

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

This handles the download, places the app in your /Applications directory, and configures the ollama binary symlink.

Method 2: Manual DMG Download

If you prefer a standard macOS installation:

  1. Download the zip file directly from ollama.com/download/mac.
  2. Unzip it and drag Ollama.app into your Applications folder.
  3. Launch the app to complete the initial setup and let it install the command-line tools.

Verifying the Installation

Once installed, verify that the CLI is fully accessible in your path:

ollama --version

To run your first model (like Llama 3.2 3B or Mistral), simply execute:

ollama run llama3.2

Note: The first run will automatically pull the model layers before launching the interactive chat interface.

Headless & Remote Access Optimization

If you plan to interact with Ollama on your Mac Mini remotely from another device on your local network, the background service defaults to listening only on localhost:11434.

To expose it to your local network, you need to update launchctl so the GUI agent reads the environment variable on boot:

  1. Set the global host environment variable: 
    launchctl setenv OLLAMA_HOST "0.0.0.0:11434"
  2. Restart Ollama: Quit the application from the macOS menu bar icon and relaunch it.
  3. Verify it's listening on all interfaces:
   lsof -i :11434

Handy Fish Aliases

To streamline managing your local instances, you can drop these quick functions or aliases into your ~/.config/fish/config.fish:

# Quick status check
alias ols="ollama list"

# Monitor active models in memory
alias ops="ollama ps"

# Completely unload models to free up unified RAM instantly
alias ofree="killall ollama"

Which model are you planning to spin up first, or are you hooking this into a specific local development sandbox?

turns.prompt_text: how can I pass images or attachments to ollama?
turns.response_html:
To pass images or visual attachments to Ollama, you must use a multimodal (vision-enabled) model. Language-only models (like standard Llama 3.2 or Mistral) will reject or ignore image inputs.

Popular vision models available on Ollama include llama3.2-vision (11B or 90B) and llava.

You can pass images using two primary workflows: directly via the Command Line (CLI) or programmatically using the REST API.

Method 1: Via the Command Line (CLI)

The Ollama CLI allows you to pass local file paths directly alongside your prompt.

Option A: Inline Command

You can pass the absolute or relative path to the image directly in a single terminal execution:

ollama run llama3.2-vision "What is written on this whiteboard? ./images/notes.png"

Option B: Interactive REPL

If you are already inside an interactive Ollama session, you can reference the path or drag and drop the file directly into your terminal window:

  1. Start the vision model: 
    ollama run llama3.2-vision
  2. Type your prompt and append the file path (or drag the file in):
   >>> Analyze this circuit diagram /Users/austin/Projects/hardware/schematic.jpg

Method 2: Via the REST API

If you are building a script, local web playground, or automation workflow, you can pass images to Ollama's API endpoints (/api/generate or /api/chat). The image must be converted into a Base64 encoded string (without the data URI prefix).

API Payload Structure

Here is an example using curl to send a request to your local Mac Mini instance:

curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{
  "model": "llama3.2-vision",
  "prompt": "Describe the architecture shown in this image.",
  "stream": false,
  "images": [
    "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAABgAAAAYCAYAAADgdz34AAAABHNCSVQICAgIfAhkiAAAAAlwSFlzAAALEwAACxMBAJqcGAAAAV5JREFUSImtlr9rVFEQxT/v..."
  ]
}'

Automation with a Fish Function

If you want a quick terminal shortcut to send an image to the local API via your Fish shell, you can add a function to read and encode the file on the fly:

function ollama-vision -d "Analyze an image using the local Ollama API"
    set -l img_path $argv[1]
    set -l prompt $argv[2]
    
    if not test -f $img_path
        echo "Error: File $img_path not found."
        return 1
    end

    # Base64 encode the image (macOS 'base64' syntax)
    set -l b64_string (base64 -i $img_path)

    # Send payload to local Ollama instance
    curl -s http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d (string join "" \
        '{"model": "llama3.2-vision", "prompt": "' $prompt '", "stream": false, "images": ["' $b64_string '"]}' \
    ) | jq '.response'
end

Usage:

ollama-vision ./print_failure.jpg "Why did this 3D print layer shift?"

Important Considerations

  • Supported File Types: Ollama natively accepts standard image formats including PNG, JPEG, and WebP.
  • Other Attachments (PDFs, CSVs, Code): Ollama does not currently parse non-image attachments (like PDFs or spreadsheets) natively via the CLI path method. For documents and code files, you must extract the text first and pass it into the prompt as a string block, or use an embedding pipeline (RAG) to handle document indexing.

turns.prompt_text: what about if I want it to have access to some directory to manipulate? Do I need to place the agent in some sort of vehicle?
turns.response_html:
Your "vehicle" metaphor is exactly how agentic architectures work. Ollama is strictly the engine—it provides the raw processing power and intelligence, but it has no limbs. On its own, it cannot see your file tree, modify files, or execute system commands unless you explicitly copy and paste the text back and forth.

To let an AI model actively traverse and manipulate a local directory, you must mount that engine into an agent execution framework (the vehicle) that exposes specific file system tools to the model.

Depending on what you want to achieve in that directory, you have a few excellent open-source vehicles to choose from.

Vehicle Options for Directory Manipulation

1. The Autonomous Pair-Programmer (Aider)

If your goal is to have the agent write code, refactor files, or structurally edit text inside a project directory, Aider is an exceptionally powerful command-line vehicle. It hooks directly into Ollama and tracks every change it makes via Git.

  • How it works: You launch it inside the target directory. It reads your files, maps out the repository structure, accepts your high-level instructions, edits the files directly, and automatically creates Git commits for every action.
  • Setup Example: First, ensure you have a tool-optimized or code-optimized model pulled in Ollama (such as qwen2.5-coder): 
    ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b
    Then, install Aider and point it to your local Ollama instance inside your shell:
    pip install aider-chat
    
    # Set the local endpoint variable for your Fish session
    set -gx OLLAMA_API_BASE http://127.0.0.1:11434
    
    # Move to your workspace and launch the vehicle
    cd ~/Projects/my-sandbox
    git init # Aider heavily relies on Git tracking
    aider --model ollama_chat/qwen2.5-coder:7b
    ```

### 2. The DIY Go-Kart (Python Native Tool Calling)
If you want to build a custom automation agent—such as a script that scans a directory, renames files based on context, or processes logs—you can construct a lightweight agent loop yourself. 

By utilizing Ollama's native tool-calling capabilities (supported well by models like Llama 3.2 and Qwen 2.5), you can provide standard Python functions as "tools" that the model can invoke.

*   **How it works:** The model analyzes your prompt, outputs a structured JSON block requesting to call a specific function (e.g., `read_directory()` or `move_file()`), your local Python script executes the actual system command, and the output is fed back to the model to determine its next action.

### 3. Full-Scale Orchestration Chassis (LangGraph / OpenHands)
For complex tasks that require a strict step-by-step state machine (e.g., *"Look at file A, if it contains an error, inspect directory B, write a patch, run a local shell script test, and repeat until successful"*), frameworks like **LangGraph** act as a robust chassis. They allow you to define advanced control loops powered entirely by local models.

---

## Essential "Seatbelts" for File-Manipulating Agents

Giving an LLM the keys to your hard drive comes with obvious risks. A model experiencing a hallucination loop could accidentally overwrite files or recursively generate garbage data. Always use these guardrails:

*   **The Git Safety Net:** Never let an agent loose in a folder that isn't a Git repository. Always run `git init` and make a clean commit before starting. If the agent makes a total mess of your directory, you can instantly wipe the slate clean:
    ```fish
    git reset --hard HEAD
    git clean -fd
    ```
*   **Directory Scoping:** Ensure your custom scripts or agent settings restrict path operations strictly to a designated `workspace/` or `sandbox/` folder rather than your root user directory.

---

What kind of manipulation tasks are you trying to automate in this directory—are we talking about a code generation sandbox, file sorting and organization, or something entirely custom?

[Local AI Agent with LangGraph and Ollama](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MAZUI4jGlU8) provides a complete walkthrough on how to set up an autonomous local reasoning agent using Ollama and LangGraph, demonstrating how to bridge the model with local tool execution loops.

turns.prompt_text: Why does aider take so much longer than just running ollama?
turns.response_html:
The latency difference you are experiencing comes down to a fundamental shift in what is happening behind the scenes. When you run ollama run, you are sending a tiny stream of text directly to the model. When you run Aider, you aren't just sending a prompt—you are launching an entire orchestration engine that forces the local model to do an immense amount of heavy lifting before it even starts typing.

Here is exactly why Aider feels significantly slower on a local Mac Mini compared to a raw Ollama session.

1. The "Prompt Pre-fill" Hit (Context Loading)

When you ask ollama run a question, your prompt might be 20 tokens long. The model processes that instantly and starts streaming.

Aider, however, is designed to understand your entire project. Before it sends your prompt to Ollama, it wraps it in a massive payload containing:

  • A Repository Map (Aider uses Tree-sitter to map out all the classes, functions, and files in your project).
  • The entire text content of any files you have explicitly added to the chat.
  • A highly detailed system prompt instructing the model how to output code modifications safely.

Your 15-word prompt suddenly becomes a 4,000+ token payload. On Apple Silicon, processing this initial chunk of data (known as the Prompt Evaluation or Pre-fill phase) requires a massive amount of sequential matrix multiplication. Until the Mac Mini finishes reading this entire context window, it cannot generate a single character of output.

2. Search-and-Replace Block Constraints

In a normal chat, a model can just ramble or stream code freely. Aider requires the model to output structural edits using a strict Search/Replace block protocol so Aider can programmatically edit your files.

For example, the model has to precisely output:

<<<<<<< SEARCH
old code
=======
new code
>>>>>>> REPLACE

Generating code in this highly constrained format forces the model to spend more compute cycles matching indentation and tracking exact syntax, which can slightly degrade generation speed (tokens per second) compared to unconstrained text generation.

3. Context Window Cache Invalidation

Ollama tries to cache the system prompt and context to speed up subsequent queries. However, every time you edit a file, run a tool, or Aider updates its repository map, the context changes.

Because the context changes between turns, Ollama often has to wipe its cache and re-evaluate the entire history and project state from scratch on the next prompt, triggering that heavy pre-fill penalty all over again.

How to Speed Up Aider Locally

If the lag is getting frustrating, you can dramatically optimize the setup with a few configuration tweaks:

  • Be aggressive with .aiderignore: If Aider is mapping your node_modules, build artifacts, .git histories, or large datasets, it will choke your context window. Create an .aiderignore file in your project root and exclude everything except the precise source files you are working on.
  • Drop files when you're done: Only keep files in the chat that are actively relevant to the current task. Use /drop filename to remove files from the immediate context when you move on to a different part of the codebase.
  • Use a faster architecture-optimized model: If you are running a heavy 14B or 32B model, drop down to qwen2.5-coder:7b or deepseek-coder:6.7b. These are heavily optimized for coding tasks and offer the best speed-to-intelligence ratio for local hardware like a Mac Mini.
  • Check your backend allocation: Ensure Ollama isn't fighting for unified RAM with other heavy processes. Running out of active RAM forces macOS to swap to disk, which absolutely tanks local LLM generation speeds.

Are you noticing the lag primarily on the very first prompt you send (the initial pause before it types), or is the actual typing speed itself painfully slow?

turns.prompt_text: Are standard copilots in vscode also this slow?
turns.response_html:
No, standard copilots (like GitHub Copilot, Cursor, or Continue using cloud keys) are significantly faster.

The difference in speed is massive, and it boils down to two main things: where the computation happens and how context is cached.

1. Cloud Infrastructure vs. Local Silos

When you use a standard extension like GitHub Copilot, your code context is bundled and securely sent to massive enterprise data centers packed with high-end server GPUs (like clusters of NVIDIA H100s or custom AI chips).

  • Local Mac Mini: Your Mac Mini has to process a 4,000+ token context window using its built-in unified memory. It processes the prompt evaluation at maybe a few dozen tokens per second, then generates text.
  • The Cloud: Cloud models can crunch through tens of thousands of context tokens in a fraction of a second (prompt pre-fill) and stream responses back to your IDE at blistering speeds (often 60–100+ tokens per second).

2. Advanced Prompt Caching

In a local environment with Aider and Ollama, if you modify a file or add a new turn to the chat, the context changes. Ollama often has to clear its cache and re-read your entire project map and history from scratch, causing that painful "long pause" before it starts typing.

Cloud providers (like Anthropic with Claude or OpenAI with GPT) use server-side prompt caching. When you send a large codebase to the cloud, the provider caches the thousands of tokens representing your repository structure. On your next prompt, the model only processes the changes or your new message. This slashes both latency and costs by up to 90%. Local engines like Ollama are getting better at context management, but they can't match server-side infrastructure yet.

3. Inline Completion vs. Agent Workflows

It's also worth separating the two types of AI features inside VS Code:

  • Inline Suggestions (Ghost Text): This is virtually instantaneous because it doesn't use a heavy reasoning model. It uses highly specialized, incredibly fast, tiny models designed to look only at the few lines surrounding your cursor.
  • Agent / Chat Modes: Standard tools now have their own "Agent" modes (like Cursor's Composer or the VS Code Copilot Agent harness) that write to multiple files and run tests. While these agent loops are slower than inline ghost text because they have to pause, think, and execute tools, they still drastically outpace a local agent due to the sheer horsepower of the cloud backend.

The Takeaway

Running things locally via Ollama and Aider gives you total data privacy, offline capability, and zero subscription limits, but you pay for it in hardware processing time. If you want that instantaneous, seamless flow state inside your IDE, cloud-backed copilot tools are still the gold standard for raw speed.

turns.prompt_text: very nice, I'll make that trade for now, what about multi-agent coding? A graph of agents? A system?
turns.response_html:
Moving from a single-agent loop like Aider to a multi-agent system is like transitioning from a solo freelancer to managing an entire specialized engineering department.

Instead of asking one model to hold the entire architecture, code generation, testing, and debugging state in its head simultaneously, you split those responsibilities across a network of narrow, specialized agents.

The industry maps these systems into three core architectural patterns.

The Three Core Architectural Paradigms

1. Graph-Based Workflows (The State Machine)

  • The Champion: LangGraph
  • The Philosophy: You treat your development pipeline as a strict, deterministic Finite State Machine. You define Nodes (which are your agents or custom code functions) and Edges (the conditional paths connecting them).
  • How it applies to coding: It is built for rigorous control. The LLM handles the reasoning inside its specific node, but the system structure dictates where the data goes next. If a piece of code fails a test node, the graph structure explicitly routes it back to the developer node.

2. Role-Based Teams (The Corporate Metaphor)

  • The Champion: CrewAI
  • The Philosophy: This framework replicates a human workplace hierarchy. You define a "crew" of individual agents, giving each a specific role, a goal, a custom backstory to shape its behavior, and precise tool access.
  • How it applies to coding: You build a squad. For example, a "Product Manager Agent" parses your requirement and writes a spec; it hands that spec sequentially to a "Senior Developer Agent" who writes the code; who then hands it to a "QA Engineer Agent" to verify the output.

3. Conversational Networks (The Group Chat)

  • The Champion: AutoGen (AG2)
  • The Philosophy: Agents solve problems by dynamically talking to each other in a shared room.
  • How it applies to coding: It relies on a multi-party debate and execution loop. A "Coder Agent" posts a Python snippet to the chat. A "Code Executor Agent" natively catches that text block, spins up a local execution sandbox, runs the script, and posts the terminal error back to the chat. A "Critic Agent" then reviews the error and suggests a fix to the coder.

Visualizing a Standard Coding Graph

A multi-agent coding system usually loops through a cyclical, self-correcting state graph rather than processing line-by-line.

Here is how a state-driven coding system handles a single feature request:

       [ User Prompt ]
              │
              ▼
    ┌───────────────────┐
    │  Planner Agent    │ <────────────────────────┐
    └─────────┬─────────┘                          │
              │ (Creates technical spec)           │
              ▼                                    │
    ┌───────────────────┐                          │
    │  Developer Agent  │                          │ (If bugs found)
    └─────────┬─────────┘                          │
              │ (Generates source code)            │
              ▼                                    │
    ┌───────────────────┐                          │
    │  Compiler/Tester  │ ───(Tests Fail)──────────┘
    └─────────┬─────────┘
              │ (Tests Pass)
              ▼
    ┌───────────────────┐
    │ Code Review Agent │ ───(Style/Security Fail)─┘
    └─────────┬─────────┘
              │ (Approved)
              ▼
       [ Clean Commit ]

The Local Reality Check: Compounding Latency

Before you stitch together a beautiful multi-agent graph on your Mac Mini, you need to calculate the Local Agent Tax.

Remember how Aider felt slow because it had to process a massive initial prompt context? In a multi-agent system, that issue compounds exponentially:

  • Context Invalidation: When Agent A (Planner) writes a 2,000-token specification and passes it to Agent B (Coder), Agent B has to read the system instructions, the original prompt, and Agent A's massive response.
  • The Pre-fill Multiplier: Ollama will have to completely re-evaluate the prompt context every single time the state transitions to a new node. A 4-agent loop resolving a single bug can easily trigger 10 to 15 sequential LLM inferences.

If a single Aider prompt takes 20 seconds of thinking time, a full multi-agent cycle through a graph locally can easily stretch into 3 to 5 minutes per task. To pull this off on local hardware without losing your mind, you typically have to drop down to incredibly lightweight, highly optimized 7B models (like qwen2.5-coder:7b) to keep token processing fast.

Are you looking to stitch together a highly structured, repeatable system (like an automated testing and patching pipeline), or are you looking for a flexible conversational team to brainstorm and prototype new features?

For a deeper look into selecting the right foundation for this type of system, you can check out this LangGraph vs. CrewAI vs. AutoGen Framework Comparison. This breakdown highlights the architectural trade-offs between strict graph-based control, conversational setups, and role-based delegation patterns when architecting multi-agent workflows.
